title: Gamma Radiation
short_intro: Gamma radiation consists of high-energy electromagnetic photons emitted from atomic nuclei during radioactive decay or nuclear transitions. These photons possess zero rest mass and zero charge, representing the excess energy of a nucleus in an excited state.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Properties of gamma rays, electromagnetic nature, comparison with alpha and beta radiations, and penetration power.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Origin of gamma rays from nuclear energy levels, internal conversion, pair production, and interaction with matter via photoelectric effect, Compton scattering, and pair production.

prerequisites: Atomic energy levels and quantum transitions

concept_notes.heading: Origin and Nature of Gamma Radiation
bullets: Gamma rays are high-frequency electromagnetic waves emitted when a daughter nucleus is left in an excited state following alpha or beta decay.
Unlike alpha and beta particles, gamma emission does not change the atomic number (Z) or mass number (A) of the nucleus.
The energy of a emitted gamma photon corresponds to the exact difference between two nuclear energy states: E = E_initial - E_final.

concept_notes.heading: Interaction of Gamma Radiation with Matter
bullets: Gamma rays interact with matter primarily through three mechanisms depending on photon energy: Photoelectric effect, Compton scattering, and Pair production.
Due to the absence of charge and mass, gamma rays have high penetrating power and low ionizing power compared to alpha and beta particles.
The intensity of gamma radiation decreases exponentially with the thickness of the absorber according to the Lambert-Beer law.

concept_notes.heading: Internal Conversion
bullets: In competition with gamma emission, an excited nucleus may directly transfer its excitation energy to an orbital electron (usually K or L shell).
This ejected orbital electron is known as an internal conversion electron, possessing kinetic energy equal to the nuclear transition energy minus the electron binding energy.
Internal conversion is followed by the emission of characteristic X-rays or Auger electrons as outer shell electrons fill the vacancy.

concept_notes.heading: Nuclear Isomerism
bullets: Some excited nuclear states have relatively long half-lives (ranging from microseconds to years) and are called nuclear isomers or metastable states.
Metastable states are denoted by the superscript 'm' next to the mass number (e.g., 99mTc).
The transition from a metastable state to the ground state via gamma emission is known as isomeric transition.

derivations.title: Exponential Attenuation Law for Gamma Rays
derivations.conditions: Monoenergetic gamma beam passing through a uniform absorber of thickness x
steps: Consider a beam of gamma photons of intensity I passing through a thin absorber layer of thickness dx.
The decrease in intensity (-dI) is directly proportional to the incident intensity I and the thickness dx: -dI = \mu I dx, where \mu is the linear attenuation coefficient.
Integrating both sides from initial intensity I_0 at x = 0 to intensity I at thickness x yields \ln(\frac{I}{I_0}) = -\mu x.

derivations.title: Threshold Energy for Pair Production
derivations.conditions: Photon interaction in the Coulomb field of a heavy nucleus where momentum and energy must be conserved
steps: Pair production involves the conversion of a gamma photon into an electron-positron pair: \gamma \rightarrow e^- + e^+.
The minimum energy (threshold energy) required is when the created electron and positron are at rest relative to the recoiling nucleus.
By conservation of rest mass energy, the minimum energy is equal to twice the rest mass energy of an electron: E_{min} = 2m_0 c^2.
Taking into account the recoil energy transferred to the massive nucleus, the exact threshold is slightly higher, but for practical purposes E_{th} \approx 1.02 \text{ MeV}.

formula_sheet.name: Gamma Photon Energy
formula_sheet.variables: h = Planck's constant, \nu = frequency, c = speed of light, \lambda = wavelength

formula_sheet.name: Radioactive Intensity Attenuation
formula_sheet.variables: I = transmitted intensity, I_0 = incident intensity, \mu = linear attenuation coefficient, x = absorber thickness
formula_sheet.units: I in W/m^2, x in m
formula_sheet.conditions: Narrow beam geometry, monoenergetic gamma rays

formula_sheet.name: Half-Value Thickness
formula_sheet.variables: x_{1/2} = thickness reducing intensity by half, \mu = linear attenuation coefficient

formula_sheet.name: Compton Wavelength Shift
formula_sheet.variables: \Delta \lambda = wavelength shift, m_0 = electron rest mass, \theta = scattering angle
formula_sheet.conditions: Elastic scattering of photon off a free electron

formula_sheet.name: Compton Electron Recoil Energy
formula_sheet.variables: E_e = kinetic energy of recoil electron, E_\gamma = incident photon energy, E_\gamma' = scattered photon energy

formula_sheet.name: Pair Production Threshold Energy
formula_sheet.variables: m_0 = rest mass of electron, c = speed of light in vacuum
formula_sheet.conditions: Presence of a neighboring nucleus for momentum conservation

formula_sheet.name: Mass Attenuation Coefficient
formula_sheet.variables: \mu = linear attenuation coefficient, \rho = density of absorber
formula_sheet.conditions: Independent of the physical state of the absorber

formula_sheet.name: Nuclear Transition Energy
formula_sheet.variables: \Delta E = energy of emitted gamma ray, E_i = initial nuclear energy level, E_f = final nuclear energy level

graphs_and_experiments.title: Absorption of Gamma Rays vs. Thickness
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A semi-logarithmic plot or standard exponential decay curve showing transmitted intensity (I) on the y-axis and absorber thickness (x) on the x-axis, showing a straight line on a ln(I) vs x plot.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The negative slope of the logarithmic plot yields the linear attenuation coefficient \mu, demonstrating the exponential nature of gamma ray absorption.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in numerical problems to calculate half-thickness or linear attenuation coefficients.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Gamma Ray Spectrum (Scintillation or Semiconductor Detector)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Counts per channel vs. Energy (MeV) displaying sharp photoelectric peaks (full energy peaks), Compton continua, and backscatter peaks.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Identifies discrete nuclear energy levels of the emitting radioisotope; photopeaks represent complete absorption of the gamma photon energy.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Interpreting pulse-height spectra and identifying radioactive isotopes based on characteristic gamma energies.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Mass Attenuation Coefficient vs. Photon Energy
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A log-log plot of mass attenuation coefficient against gamma energy, showing three distinct dominant regions: photoelectric (low energy), Compton scattering (intermediate energy), and pair production (high energy).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates the dominance of different interaction mechanisms across various energy ranges.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual questions regarding which interaction mechanism dominates at specific gamma ray energies.

solved_numericals.question: A gamma-ray beam has an initial intensity of 1000 units. After passing through a lead sheet of thickness 10 cm, its intensity drops to 125 units. Calculate the linear attenuation coefficient of lead.
solution_steps: Use the attenuation formula: I = I_0 e^{-\mu x}.
Take natural logarithms on both sides: \ln(1/8) = -10\mu \implies -\ln(8) = -10\mu \implies -2.079 = -10\mu.

solved_numericals.question: Find the wavelength of a gamma photon emitted during a nuclear transition with an energy release of 2.48 MeV.
solution_steps: Convert energy from MeV to Joules: E = 2.48 \times 10^6 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J} = 3.968 \times 10^{-13} \text{ J}.
Substitute constants h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s} and c = 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}: \lambda = \frac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34}) (3 \times 10^8)}{3.968 \times 10^{-13}}.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the half-value thickness (x_1_2) of a material whose linear attenuation coefficient is 0.0693 m^-1.
solution_steps: Recall the formula for half-value thickness: x_{1/2} = \frac{\ln(2)}{\mu}.

assumptions_and_limitations: Gamma ray attenuation equations assume a parallel, monoenergetic, and narrow beam of photons; broad beam geometries require buildup factors to account for scattered radiation.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Gamma rays change the atomic number of the emitting nucleus.
common_misconceptions.correct: Gamma emission leaves both the atomic number (Z) and mass number (A) unchanged.
common_misconceptions.why: Gamma rays are pure electromagnetic radiation emitted due to a drop in nuclear energy state, unlike alpha or beta decays which involve particle emission changing nuclear composition.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Gamma rays have mass and charge.
common_misconceptions.correct: Gamma rays are massless and chargeless photons.
common_misconceptions.why: They are packets of electromagnetic energy (photons), possessing momentum and energy but no rest mass or electric charge.

quick_revision: Gamma rays are electromagnetic waves originating from nuclear de-excitation with zero mass and zero charge, traveling at the speed of light.
Radioactive Intensity Attenuation: I = I_0 e^{-\mu x}
